tasks.short: Schedule qualification tests, prepare and mark written tests, observe practical tests, decide pass or fail and update the register.

steps.what: Inspector schedules qualification tests: by e-mail with operators and their supervisors today; after the change by picking test slots in the LMS for the operators it lists as due
Inspector checks the invitations before they go: the operators really due, test type, date and the supervisors copied
Inspector sends the checked invitations from the LMS
Inspector puts together the written test from the question bank
Operator takes the written test
Inspector marks the written test by hand
Inspector observes the operator using the equipment in a practical test
Inspector decides whether operators are qualified and signs the result
Inspector updates the qualification register spreadsheet with result and expiry

tasks.design: Qualifications with expiry dates live in the {LMS}, which lists operators due for a test and draws the written test from the question bank; the inspector picks slots, checks the invitations and sends them once; closed questions are marked automatically. The practical test, the pass or fail decision and the signature stay with the inspector, whose result is entered once and updates the register and next due date.
tasks.previous_blocker: The register was a spreadsheet, so tests were scheduled, marked and recorded by hand.
tasks.enabler_now: Learning systems hold qualifications with expiry dates, question banks and automatic marking of closed questions.
tasks.still_hard: Practical competence can only be judged by watching; qualification records are personal data under works council rules.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing whether an operator really handles the equipment safely under pressure.

ambition.what: No operator working on equipment with an expired qualification, because tests are invited before expiry.

tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in decision rights; test admin shrinks.

reach.task: Plan qualification refreshers across the plant
reach.learn: Whether expiry-driven invitations smooth the training calendar.

evidence.claim: Learning systems hold qualifications with expiry dates, question banks and automatic marking of closed questions.
Rules on processing staff personal data and systems able to monitor performance need works council consent.

assumptions: Boundary: from scheduling tests to the register updated; training courses are outside.

Input contract: qualification types, expiry periods and question banks kept by the training coordinator with quality; fallback is the spreadsheet register; existing qualification records are last cycle's register entries with expiry dates.
Operator time on tests is outside the inspector's savings.

Practical tests, decisions, the invitation check and the send keep their full time; no model judges operators. s1 keeps 40 for picking slots and agreeing changes; s2 keeps 30 for choosing questions; s4 keeps 20 for checking auto-marked results and marking open questions; s7 keeps 30 for entering the result once. Qualification records are personal data, so the LMS setup goes to the works council first.
unknowns: Number of qualification tests per year.
Share of closed questions in the written tests.
research_questions: Do lapsed qualifications fall after expiry-driven invitations?

already_counted.description: Inspector checks auto-marked results and marks open questions.

incremental.description: Inspector keeps the question bank current.
Training coordinator keeps qualification types and expiry rules current.

approvals.approved_version: The test invitations with operator, test type and date exactly as checked by the inspector in s1b, sent once from the LMS to those operators and their supervisors; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: few qualified roles and mostly open questions, so scheduling and marking stay largely by hand (21.1); high: question banks and expiry rules in the LMS as assumed (32.6).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Watch automatic inspection and sorting machines, run challenge parts, log readings, re-check rejects and call the technician on drift.

steps.what: Inspector monitors machines that automatically measure, sort or inspect products and their reject rate
Inspector runs known good and bad challenge parts through the machine at shift start
Inspector logs machine readings and challenge results: on a paper log today; after the change readings come from the machine controller and the inspector enters the challenge results on a tablet
Inspector re-checks rejected parts by hand
Inspector checks a drift alarm before it goes: the drift is real and not a measurement error, the machine and the values out of limit
Inspector sends the checked drift notice to the technician: by phone today, from the SPC screen with the chart after the change
Maintenance technician adjusts or recalibrates the machine

tasks.design: The inspection machine's measurements and reject counts feed statistical process control in the {OPS_SYSTEM}, with control charts and alarms that notify the inspector when the process drifts; the inspector checks the drift and sends it once to the technician. Challenge-part results are entered on a tablet against the machine, so the paper log disappears; challenge runs and re-checks of rejects stay manual.
tasks.previous_blocker: Machine readings were copied by hand onto paper logs, and drift was noticed by eye.
tasks.enabler_now: SPC software reads gauges and machine controllers, draws control charts and raises alarms.
tasks.still_hard: Re-checking rejects needs a trained eye; logs per operator need works council consent.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing when a machine is rejecting good parts or passing bad ones before the chart shows it.

ambition.what: Drift caught within minutes on every shift instead of at the next log check.

tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in decision rights; the inspector watches charts instead of copying readings.

reach.task: Set control limits for inspection machines
reach.learn: Whether alarm rates show limits set too tight.

evidence.claim: SPC software reads gauges, measuring machines and controllers, draws control charts and raises alarms.
An automotive supplier inspects all moulded light panels in line with a visual inspection system; about 95% of inspection is automated (vendor reference, no baseline).
Per-operator logs can monitor staff and need works council consent.

assumptions: Boundary: from monitoring the machine to recalibration; setting control limits is outside.

Input contract: measurements and reject counts from the machine controller connected by maintenance; control limits set by the quality engineer; challenge results entered by the inspector; fallback is the paper log.
Data is logged per machine, not per operator.
Technician time is outside the inspector's savings.

Challenge runs, re-checks and the drift check keep their full time. s1 keeps 70 because alarms replace part of the watching; s3 keeps 40 because challenge results are still entered by the inspector; s5 keeps 50 for sending the notice instead of a call.
unknowns: Whether the machines can export measurements.
How often drift occurs per week.
research_questions: Do alarms shorten the time from drift to recalibration?

incremental.description: Inspector checks that the machine data feed is running.
Quality engineer sets and reviews control limits.

approvals.approved_version: The drift notice with machine, chart and out-of-limit values exactly as checked by the inspector in s5b, sent once to the maintenance technician on duty through the SPC system; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: older machines without data export keep paper logs and need watching (10.0); high: machine controllers connected as assumed (21.7).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Take compliance questions, find the rule or procedure, interpret it for the case, write and send advice, and explain safety on site.

steps.what: Contractors, engineers and owners enter their compliance question in the web form
Inspector takes questions from contractors, engineers and owners: by e-mail and phone today; after the change from the logged form, with phone calls logged by the inspector
Inspector looks up the legal requirements, standard or company procedure
Inspector interprets how the requirement applies to this case
Inspector writes the advice and recommended compliance procedures

loop.input: The question, the inspector's interpretation notes and the retrieved paragraphs from the approved compliance library.
loop.output: A short advice letter with the steps to take, each citing the library paragraph and its version date.
loop.check: Every requirement in the draft must cite a paragraph from the approved library that the inspector confirms says it, in its current version; the inspector also reads the draft against the question and their interpretation: does it answer what was asked, fit the case and state its limits; a requirement without a citation or a sentence that does not fit is rewritten by the inspector.
loop.stop: One draft and one redraft; then the inspector writes the letter.
loop.why_not_simpler: Turning several rules and the inspector's notes into clear steps for an outsider is writing; a template only holds the letterhead.

steps.what: Inspector checks the final letter: it answers the question, fits the case, each cited paragraph says what the letter claims and is current, and the recipient is right
Inspector signs and sends the checked advice letter: by e-mail today, by one send from the document system after the change
Inspector explains safety information to craft workers on site

tasks.design: Questions come in through a form that logs them; a search over the company's approved compliance library in {DOCS} (procedures, summaries of standards and regulations, each with a version date) returns the relevant paragraphs. A bounded step drafts the advice letter citing those paragraphs; the inspector reads it against the question and the case, checks the final letter and signs and sends it once; interpretation and site briefings stay with the inspector.
tasks.previous_blocker: Rules were spread over binders and shared drives, and every letter was written from scratch.
tasks.enabler_now: Search over a curated document library and drafting with required citations are now cheap to build.
tasks.still_hard: Interpretation of edge cases is the job; the library must be kept current as rules change, such as the new machinery rules from January 2027.
tasks.human_edge: Explaining to a contractor why a rule matters, and when a situation needs stricter care than the letter of the rule.

ambition.what: Written advice with sources for every question, not only for formal requests.

tasks.altitude: The inspector checks and signs drafted advice; interpretation stays theirs.

reach.task: Answer staff questions on safety procedures
reach.learn: Whether the same library and citations serve internal questions.

evidence.claim: Search over a curated library with drafting that must cite paragraphs can support written advice.
The EU machinery regulation applies from 14 January 2027 and requires third-party assessment for safety components with self-learning behaviour.
No AI Act annex III point covers this kind of drafting support.

assumptions: Boundary: from receiving a question to advice sent and explained on site; enforcement is outside.

Input contract: approved compliance library with version dates kept by the compliance officer; questions logged through the form or by the inspector from calls; fallback is searching binders and writing by hand.
Outside parties' time is outside the inspector's savings.

Interpretation, site briefings and the final check keep their full time. s1 keeps 60 because phone questions remain and only noting written ones goes; s2 keeps 50 for reading the retrieved paragraphs; s4 keeps 60 because the inspector reads and corrects every drafted sentence; s5 keeps 20 for signing and sending. The asker's form entry (s1q) is outside the inspector's savings.
unknowns: Number of compliance questions per month.
How current the company's procedures are.
research_questions: How often does the inspector reject a drafted citation as not supporting the statement?

already_counted.description: Inspector checks retrieved paragraphs for relevance and version.
Inspector checks every citation in the drafted letter before signing.

incremental.description: Inspector flags missing topics in the library.
Compliance officer keeps the library current with rule changes.

approvals.approved_version: The advice letter exactly as checked and signed by the inspector in s4c, sent once to the contractor, engineer or owner who asked the question; any edit needs a new check and signature.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: many questions are about unusual installations with no library coverage, so research and writing stay mostly by hand (17.1); high: the library covers most questions as assumed (29.5).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Count or weigh incoming shipments, sample and inspect, compute the usable amount, record it and report shortfalls to purchasing.

steps.what: Inspector counts or weighs items in shipments on arrival
Inspector takes samples and inspects them for defects
Inspector computes usable amounts from counts, rejects and the sampling plan with a calculator
Inspector records counts and defects: written on the receiving form and typed into the ERP today, entered once on the tablet after the change
Inspector checks the goods receipt before posting: counts, defects and the computed usable amount against the shipment and the sampling plan
Inspector posts the checked goods receipt with the usable quantity
Inspector prepares the shortfall notice for purchasing: written by e-mail today; generated from the posted receipt after the change, with the inspector's note on the defects
Inspector checks the shortfall notice: article, supplier, ordered, received and usable quantities and the defects found
Inspector sends the checked shortfall notice to purchasing
Buyer files the claim with the supplier

tasks.design: Configure incoming inspection in the {ERP} quality module with the sampling plan per article: the inspector enters counts and defects once on a tablet, the usable quantity is computed, and the inspector checks the goods receipt and posts it once; a shortfall produces a notice with the figures, which the inspector checks and sends once to purchasing. Counting, weighing and inspecting stay manual.
tasks.previous_blocker: Usable amounts were worked out on paper and typed into the ERP later.
tasks.enabler_now: ERP quality modules hold sampling plans and compute acceptance from entered results.
tasks.still_hard: Sampling plans must match supplier agreements; some defects need judgement on whether parts are still usable.
tasks.human_edge: Deciding whether a borderline defect makes a part unusable.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in decision rights; arithmetic and retyping go.

reach.learn: Whether same-day notices raise the share of claims accepted.

evidence.claim: SPC and quality software reads results and computes defect percentages with a link to the ERP quality module.
Arithmetic tasks such as defect percentages are formulas in quality or ERP software, configured rather than built.

assumptions: Boundary: from arrival to the supplier claim raised; payment is outside.
Input contract: sampling plans per article set by the quality engineer in the ERP; counts and defects entered by the inspector; fallback is the paper form.
Buyer time is outside the inspector's savings.

Counting, weighing, inspection, both checks, the posting and the send keep their full time. s4 keeps 50 because counts and defects are still entered once and only typing the paper form goes; s5 keeps 40 for the note on the defects.
unknowns: Number of incoming shipments per day.
Whether the ERP quality module is licensed.
research_questions: Do claims reach suppliers faster with automatic shortfall notices?

already_counted.description: Inspector checks the computed usable amount before posting.

incremental.description: Inspector handles tablet and posting errors.
Quality engineer keeps sampling plans current.

approvals.approved_version: The goods receipt with counts, defects and usable quantity exactly as checked by the inspector in s4b, posted once against the purchase order in the {ERP}; any correction needs a new check and posting.

The shortfall notice with article, supplier, ordered, received and usable quantities and defects exactly as checked by the inspector in s5b, sent once to purchasing for a supplier claim; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: many shipments need full counts and judgement on usability, so entries and notices stay largely by hand (21.9); high: sampling plans set per article as assumed (27.1).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The inspector keeps inspecting, judging and explaining; logs, arithmetic, registers and letters become automatic or drafted.
role.ambitious_version: An inspector who spots drift within minutes and answers every compliance question in writing with sources.

job.title: Inspectors, Testers, Sorters, Samplers, and Weighers
